claim: Kung and Robinson 1981 (analytic bound, not measured): for d = 3, m = 199 and n = 10^4 the probability that one insertion restarts a concurrent insertion is below 0.0007, for large B-trees.
Kung and Robinson 1981 name starvation as the major difficulty of optimistic concurrency control and say it can be solved by using locking (stated, not measured).

Larson et al. 2012 (main-memory engines, 12 cores, 2 NUMA nodes): at low contention (10M rows, 10 reads and 2 writes per transaction) single-version locking reaches over 2M transactions per second, and MV/L has 30 percent lower throughput than MV/O.
evidence: arXiv 1201.0228 (as the collect file gives it)

claim: Larson et al. 2012 (main-memory engines): when 80 percent of transactions are read-only, the two multiversion schemes reach 63 and 73 percent higher throughput than the single-version engine 1V.
evidence: arXiv 1201.0228 (as the collect file gives it)

claim: Larson et al. 2012 (main-memory engines, long readers at x = 1 and x = 12 as the collect file gives them): at x = 1 update throughput drops 75 percent for the single-version engine and 5 percent for the multiversion schemes; at x = 12 the multiversion engine has 80 times higher update throughput than 1V.
evidence: arXiv 1201.0228 (as the collect file gives it)
handles: snapshot readers do not block writers

claim: Larson et al. 2012 (main-memory engines): serializability costs the two multiversion schemes 10 to 19 percent lower throughput.
evidence: arXiv 1201.0228 (as the collect file gives it)

claim: Diaconu et al. 2013, Hekaton in SQL Server (self-reported, the company's own figures): on a contended insert workload (60 streams, 50 percent update and 50 percent read-only, 100 rows inserted per update, 12 cores) throughput reaches 7,709 transactions per second through interop (3.3 times plain SQL Server) and 36,375 through compiled stored procedures (15.7 times in total).
Diaconu et al. 2013 (self-reported): on plain SQL Server, latch contention limits CPU utilisation to 40 percent for more than 6 cores in the same workload.
Diaconu et al. 2013 (self-reported): the paper states a 20 times speedup when doing 10 or more lookups per call, in single-thread CPU cycles; the baseline is not restated in the collect file.
Tu et al. 2013 (Silo): on a standard TPC-C workload mix on a 32-core machine, Silo achieves almost 700,000 transactions per second with near-linear scalability.
Tu et al. 2013 (Silo): per-core transaction throughput at 32 cores is 91 percent of that at 8 cores.
Tu et al. 2013 (Silo): with a shared global transaction-id counter, throughput collapses after 24 workers, and the key-value variant outperforms MemSilo plus GlobalTID by 1.80 times at 32 workers.

Tu et al. 2013 (Silo): against partition locks under cross-partition load, Partitioned-Store beats MemSilo by 1.54 times with no cross-partition transactions, falls below it at roughly 20 percent cross-partition, and MemSilo beats it by 2.98 times at roughly 60 percent.
Tu et al. 2013 (Silo): with a hot counter taken out of the transaction, throughput is 17.21 times higher at 32 workers and 8.20 times at 24 workers; the collect file does not restate the baseline.
Yu et al. 2016 (TicToc), abstract: up to 92 percent higher throughput and 3.3 times lower abort rate than previous algorithms, on a 40-core machine with 80 threads and a 10M-record YCSB table.

Yu et al. 2016 (TicToc): on TPC-C with 4 warehouses (high contention) TicToc achieves 1.8 times the throughput of Silo and cuts its abort rate by 27 percent; the advantage disappears at 80 warehouses.
Yu et al. 2016 (TicToc): on medium-contention YCSB (theta 0.8, 16 queries, 90 percent reads) throughput is similar to Silo and the abort rate is 3.3 times lower.
handles: TicToc medium contention YCSB abort rate

claim: Yu et al. 2016 (TicToc): on high-contention YCSB (theta 0.9, 50 percent writes) the timestamp policy does not reduce the abort rate, and without the optimisations TicToc is only 10 percent better than Silo.

Yu et al. 2016 (TicToc): at medium contention, dropping from serializable to repeatable read gains 4.7 percent for TicToc and 5.6 percent for Silo, against 67.4 percent for DL_DETECT and 200.0 percent for NO_WAIT.

Lim et al. 2017 (Cicada, self-contained single 28-core machine): Cicada reaches 3 times the throughput of the next fastest scheme on contended TPC-C (1 and 4 warehouses, up to 28 threads) and 1.37 times on contended YCSB, and up to 69.2 percent higher on uncontended YCSB.
Lim et al. 2017 (Cicada): on YCSB (16 requests, 50 percent read-modify-write, Zipf 0.99) with 28 threads, Cicada throughput is 37.1 percent higher than TicToc.

Lim et al. 2017 (Cicada): high abort rates are not necessarily harmful when aborts are inexpensive, but the paper also says aborts can be expensive and that the best maximum backoff is workload dependent, often zero.
Tanabe et al. 2020 (CCBench, 224 threads; the text gives no percentage): Wait began to outperform NoWait as transaction size increased, because abort-retry cost grows with transaction length.
Tanabe et al. 2020 (CCBench): when the write ratio rose from 0 to 10 percent the abort rate rose rapidly and performance fell, because write operations produce many read validation failures.
Tanabe et al. 2020 (CCBench): under MVCC, a single long transaction in the workload stops even state-of-the-art garbage collection from holding down the number of versions.
Tanabe et al. 2020 (CCBench, one platform): in one high-skew read-heavy case Silo and TicToc outperformed Cicada; Tanabe attributes the difference from Cicada's own result to different platforms.

Harding et al. 2017 (distributed, 16 to 64 servers on EC2): protocol throughput is relatively unaffected by skew up to theta 0.5, and at theta 0.8 all but one protocol converge to the same low performance.
Harding et al. 2017 (distributed, theta 0.6, 100 percent updates): NO_WAIT performs 54 percent better than the next-best non-deterministic protocol, OCC.
Harding et al. 2017 (distributed): at a 10 percent update rate under WAIT_DIE there is an average of 1.4 aborts per transaction.
Harding et al. 2017 (distributed): OCC performs worse than the other non-deterministic protocols under low contention because of validation and copying overhead, but better at higher contention.

Yu et al. 2014 (simulated DBx1000, up to 1024 cores, YCSB): without skew throughput scales almost linearly; at theta 0.6 it peaks at several hundred cores and then falls from thrashing; at theta 0.8 it peaks at 16 cores.
handles: thrashing medium contention several hundred cores

claim: Yu et al. 2014 (simulated, 1024 cores, theta 0.8): OCC performs best because one transaction is always allowed to commit even though many abort in validation.
Yu et al. 2014 (simulated, theta 0.6 with writes): OCC spends a large portion of its time aborting transactions and does not perform as well as the alternatives.
handles: OCC worse with writes medium contention

claim: Yu et al. 2014 (simulated, short transactions): DL_DETECT and NO_WAIT have the best performance and OCC the worst.
Yu et al. 2014 (simulated, partitioned H-STORE): best for single-partition uniform work up to 800 cores, but it does not scale with transactions accessing four or more partitions.
Yu et al. 2014 (simulated, TPC-C with fewer warehouses than cores): all schemes fail to scale.
Yu et al. 2014 (simulated): MVCC has the best performance when there are only a small number of write transactions.
Zhou et al. 2021 (FoundationDB, self-reported, production multi-tenant workload): the transaction conflict rate is below 1 percent, OCC works well, and a conflicting client restarts its transaction.
Zhou et al. 2021 (FoundationDB, self-reported): one single-threaded resolver handles 280K transactions per second, each reading one random key range and writing another.

Zhou et al. 2021 (FoundationDB, self-reported): on 24 machines with 22 proxies and 336 storage servers throughput scales linearly with operations per second, and resolvers and proxies saturate at 2 million operations per second.
Zhou et al. 2021 (FoundationDB): the MVCC window is 5 seconds; a transaction past the limit is usually inefficient, and long jobs should be divided into smaller transactions.

PostgreSQL manual chapter 13.2: at repeatable read, an update of a row changed since the snapshot fails with could not serialize access due to concurrent update, and applications must be prepared to retry transactions.
handles: could not serialize access concurrent update

claim: PostgreSQL manual chapter 13.2: at serializable, predicate locks do not cause any blocking and flag dangerous read-write dependencies.
